cards.front: What are the two main problems to discover the functions of living matter?
cards.back: In a living plant and in a living animal
cards.source_quote:
Problems.--To discover the functions of living matter.
          (a) In a living plant.
          (  b) In a living animal.

cards.front: What type of plant is recommended for laboratory study of a living plant?
cards.back: A weed
cards.source_quote:
Laboratory study of a living plant.--Any whole plant may
       be used; a weed is preferable.

cards.front: What is a laboratory demonstration for the functions of a living animal?
cards.back: The growth of pollen tubes
cards.source_quote: Demonstration.--The growth of pollen tubes.

cards.front: What is a laboratory exercise for the growth of the mature ovary?
cards.back: The growth of the mature ovary into the fruit, e.g. bean or pea pod
cards.source_quote:
Laboratory exercise.--The growth of the mature ovary into
       the fruit, e.g. bean or pea pod.

cards.front: What are some examples of weeds that are particularly well fitted by nature to produce many of their kind?
cards.back: The dandelion, butter and eggs, the shepherd's purse
cards.source_quote: Such plants--the dandelion, butter and eggs, the shepherd's purse--are particularly well fitted by nature to produce many of their kind, and by this means drive out other plants which cannot do this so well.

cards.cloze_text: A walk into the fields or any vacant lot on a day in the early fall will give us first-hand acquaintance with many common plants which, because of their ability to grow under somewhat unfavorable conditions, are called {{c1::weeds}}.

cards.front: What is the term for each part of a living plant or animal that has a separate work to do?
cards.back: organ
cards.source_quote: Each part of the living plant or animal which has a separate work to do is called an organ.

cards.front: What are plants and animals collectively referred to as?
cards.back: living organisms
cards.source_quote: plants and animals are spoken of as living organisms.

cards.front: What is the example given for a part of a plant?
cards.back: stem
cards.source_quote: as the stem of the plant or the leg of the insect

cards.front: What is the example given for a part of an insect?
cards.back: leg
cards.source_quote: as the stem of the plant or the leg of the insect

cards.front: What is the purpose of the illustration mentioned in the passage?
cards.back: to show a weed in an unfavorable environment
cards.source_quote: [Illustration: A weed--notice the unfavorable environment.]

cards.front: What is the relationship between parts of a living plant or animal and the whole?
cards.back: Each part is a part of the whole living plant or animal
cards.source_quote: Each part of the living plant or animal which has a separate work to do is called an organ.

cards.front: What is the function of the root in a plant?
cards.back: The root holds the plant firmly in the ground and takes in water and mineral matter from the soil; the stem holds the leaves up to the: the stem holds the leaves up to the light and acts as a pathway for fluids between the root and leaves; the leaves, under certain conditions, manufacture food for the plant and breathe; the flowers form the fruits; the fruits hold the seeds, which in turn hold young plants which are capable of reproducing adult plants of the same kind. (This seems to be a mistake in the passage. The correct function of the root is: The root holds the plant firmly in the ground and takes in water and mineral matter from the soil.)

cards.front: What are the three parts of the grasshopper's body?
cards.back: Head, middle part, and hind part of the body (jointed body composed of a middle and a hind part).
cards.source_quote: The grasshopper has a head, a jointed body composed of a middle and a hind part

cards.front: What are the grasshopper's legs and wings used for?
cards.back: Movement
cards.source_quote: Obviously, the wings and legs are used for movement

cards.front: How does the grasshopper breathe?
cards.back: Breathing movements are taking place in the hind part of the animal
cards.source_quote: a careful watching of the hind part of the animal shows us that breathing movements are taking place

cards.front: What does the grasshopper eat?
cards.back: Grass
cards.source_quote: a bit of grass placed before it may be eaten, the tiny black jaws biting little pieces out of the grass

cards.front: How does the grasshopper react when disturbed?
cards.back: It hops away
cards.source_quote: If disturbed, the insect hops away

cards.front: How does the grasshopper react when trying to get it?
cards.back: It jumps or flies away
cards.source_quote: if we try to get it, it jumps or flies away

cards.cloze_text: The grasshopper moves, {{c1::breathes}}, feeds, and has sensation, while apparently the plant does none of these.
cards.source_quote: The animal moves, breathes, feeds, and has sensation, while apparently the plant does none of these.

cards.front: What is the purpose of later chapters according to the passage?
cards.back: To prove that the functions of plants and animals are in many respects similar and that both plants and animals breathe, feed, and reproduce.
cards.source_quote: It will be the purpose of later chapters to prove that the functions of plants and animals are in many respects similar and that both plants and animals breathe, feed, and reproduce.

cards.front: What is the term for the smallest units of building material of the plant or animal revealed by the compound microscope?
cards.back: cells
cards.source_quote: These smallest units of building material of the plant or animal disclosed by the compound microscope are called cells.

cards.front: What is the function of the veins in a leaf?
cards.back: They form a framework for the flat blade, similar to how sticks hold paper in a kite.
cards.source_quote: Here it splits up into a network of tiny "veins" which evidently form a framework for the flat blade somewhat as the sticks of a kite hold the paper in place.

cards.front: What is the structure that holds the flat, expanded blade of a leaf away from the branch?
cards.back: A little stalk
cards.source_quote: Holding the flat, expanded blade away from the branch is a little stalk, which extends into the blade of the leaf.

cards.front: What are the two surfaces of a leaf called in the context of this passage?
cards.back: Upper surface and lower surface
cards.source_quote: e, cells of the upper surface; d, cells of the lower surface; i, air spaces in the leaf; v, vein in cross sections; p, green cells.

cards.front: What is the primary difference in the composition of a leaf's materials?
cards.back: The leaf is much thinner and more delicate in some parts than in others.
cards.source_quote: The leaf is much thinner and more delicate in some parts than in others.

cards.cloze_text: These smallest units of building material of the plant or animal disclosed by the compound microscope are called {{c1::cells}}.

cards.front: What is a tissue in the context of plant biology?
cards.back: A collection of cells that are more or less alike in size and shape, forming parts of the plant such as veins, the flat blade, or other portions.
cards.source_quote: Tissues.[2]--The cells which form certain parts of the veins, the flat blade, or other portions of the: the plant, are often found in groups or collections, the cells of which are more or less alike in size and shape. Such a collection of cells is called a tissue.

cards.front: What are examples of tissues in plants?
cards.back: The cells covering the outside of the human body, muscle cells, bony tissues, and many others.
cards.source_quote: Examples of tissues are the cells covering the outside of the human body, the muscle cells, which collectively allow of movement, bony tissues which form the framework to which the muscles are attached, and many others.

cards.cloze_text: Tissues.[2]--The cells which form certain parts of the veins, the flat blade, or other portions of the plant, are often found in groups or collections, the cells of which are more or less alike in size and shape. Such a collection of cells is {{c1::tissue}}.

cards.back: To form parts of the plant such as veins, the flat blade, or other portions.

cards.back: A collection of cells that are more or less alike in size and shape, forming parts of the plant.

cards.front: What plant tissue can be used to demonstrate the cell?
cards.back: Epidermal cells from a frog or scraped from the inside of one's mouth, onion skin stained with tincture of iodine, young bean or pea stem, or Elodea leaf cells
cards.source_quote: Any simple plant or animal tissue can be used to demonstrate the cell.

cards.front: How can epidermal cells be obtained for cell demonstration?
cards.back: By stripping them from the body of a frog or by scraping the inside of one's mouth
cards.source_quote: Epidermal cells may be stripped from the body of the frog or obtained by scraping the inside of one's mouth.

cards.front: What plant tissue shows well when stained with tincture of iodine?
cards.back: Onion skin
cards.source_quote: The thin skin from an onion stained with tincture of iodine shows well,

cards.front: Which plant tissues are good for demonstrating cell structure?
cards.back: Thin sections of a young bean or pea stem
cards.source_quote: as do thin sections of a young stem, as the bean or pea.

cards.front: What is a good place to study tissue and its cells?
cards.back: The leaf of a green water plant, Elodea
cards.source_quote: One of the best places to study a tissue and the cells of which it is composed is in the leaf of a green water plant, Elodea.

cards.front: Why are Elodea cells good for cell study?
cards.back: The cells are large, and the movement of living matter within the cells can be easily seen
cards.source_quote: In this plant the cells are large, and not only their outline, but the movement of the living matter within the cells, may easily be seen,

cards.front: What is a cell defined as?
cards.back: A tiny mass of living matter containing a nucleus, either living alone or forming a unit of the building material of a living thing.
cards.source_quote: A cell may be defined as a tiny mass of living matter containing a nucleus, either living alone or forming a unit of the building material of a living thing.

cards.front: What is protoplasm?
cards.back: The living matter of which all cells are formed.
cards.source_quote: The living matter of which all cells are formed is known as protoplasm (formed from two Greek words meaning first form).

cards.front: What do we see when examining Elodea under a compound microscope?
cards.back: A number of structures resembling bricks in a wall.
cards.source_quote: If we examine under a compound microscope a small bit of the water plant Elodea, we see a number of structures resembling bricks in a wall.

cards.front: What is the material inside the cell wall of Elodea cells?
cards.back: The protoplasm of the cell.
cards.source_quote: This moving substance is living matter, the protoplasm of the cell.

cards.front: What are the green bodies in Elodea cells?
cards.back: Chlorophyll bodies.
cards.source_quote: The green bodies (the chlorophyll bodies) we shall learn more about later; they are found only in plant cells.

cards.front: What structure is found in all plant and animal cells?
cards.back: A nucleus (pl. nuclei).
cards.source_quote: All plant and animal cells appear to be alike in the fact that every living cell possesses a structure known as the nucleus (pl. nuclei), which is found within the body of the cell.

cards.cloze_text: Within the nucleus of all cells are found certain bodies called {{c1::chromosomes}}.
cards.source_quote: Within the nucleus of all cells are found certain bodies called chromosomes.

cards.cloze_text: These chromosomes in a given plant or animal are always constant in number. These chromosomes are supposed to be the bearers of the {{c1::inheritable qualities}} which make the offspring like its parents.
cards.source_quote: These chromosomes are supposed to be the bearers of the qualities which we believe can be handed down from plant to plant and from animal to animal, in other words, the inheritable qualities which make the offspring like its parents.

cards.front: How do cells grow and divide?
cards.back: Cells grow to a certain size and then split into two new cells through fission, where the nucleus divides first, followed by chromosome division and separation of protoplasm.
cards.source_quote: How Cells form Others.--Cells grow to a certain size and then split into two new cells.

cards.front: What is the first step in cell division?
cards.back: The nucleus divides first.
cards.source_quote: In this process, which is of very great importance in the growth of both plants and animals, the nucleus divides first.

cards.front: How do chromosomes divide during cell division?
cards.back: Each chromosome splits lengthwise, with the parts going in equal numbers to each of the two new cells.
cards.source_quote: The chromosomes also divide, each splitting lengthwise and the parts going in equal numbers to each of the two cells formed from the old cell.

cards.front: What happens after the nucleus and chromosomes divide?
cards.back: The rest of the protoplasm separates, forming two new cells.
cards.source_quote: Then the rest of the protoplasm separates, and two new cells are formed.

cards.cloze_text: Cells grow to a certain size and then {{c1::split}} into two new cells.
cards.source_quote: How Cells form Others.--Cells grow to a certain size and then split into two new cells.

cards.cloze_text: In this process, which is of very great importance in the growth of both plants and animals, the {{c1::nucleus}} divides first.
cards.source_quote: In this process, which is of very great importance in the growth of both plants and animals, the nucleus divides first.

cards.cloze_text: The chromosomes also divide, each {{c1::splitting}} lengthwise and the parts going in equal numbers to each of the two cells formed from the old cell.
cards.source_quote: The chromosomes also divide, each splitting lengthwise and the parts going in equal numbers to each of the two cells formed from the old cell.

cards.cloze_text: This process is known as {{c1::fission}}.
cards.source_quote: This process is known as fission.

cards.front: What part of the cell divides first?
cards.back: The nucleus (or cell nucleus) divides first in the cell division process.
cards.source_quote: Which part of the cell divides first? What seems to become of the chromosomes?

cards.front: What happens to the chromosomes during cell division?
cards.back: The chromosomes are separated and distributed to the two daughter cells.
cards.source_quote: Which part of the cell divides first? What seems to become of the chromosomes?

cards.front: What are some examples of very large cells?
cards.back: Root hairs of plants and eggs of some animals.
cards.source_quote: There are cells so large that they can easily be seen with the unaided eye; for example, the root hairs of plants and eggs of some animals.

cards.front: What are some examples of very small cells?
cards.back: Bacteria (plant cells) and other microscopic cells found in milk.
cards.source_quote: On the other hand, cells may be so minute, as in the case of the plant cells named bacteria, that several million might be present in a few drops of milk.

cards.front: What are the different shapes of cells?
cards.back: Cubes, columns, spheres, flat plates, or extremely irregular shapes.
cards.source_quote: The forms of cells may be extremely varied in different tissues; they may assume the form of cubes, columns, spheres, flat plates, or may be extremely irregular in shape.

cards.front: What is an example of a cell that is so small it is invisible to the naked eye?
cards.back: Nervous system cells in humans and other large animals (e.g., ox, elephant, whale).
cards.source_quote: One kind of tissue cell, found in man, has a body so small as to be quite invisible to the naked eye, although it has a prolongation several feet in length. Such are some of the cells of the nervous system of man and other large animals, as the ox, elephant, and whale.

cards.front: What are some examples of organisms that are made up of collections of cells?
cards.back: Some small flowerless plants or tiny animals living in fresh or salt water, such as those barely visible to the eye, are examples of organisms made up of collections of cells. The large plants and animals like California trees and elephants are also made up of collections of cells but are not necessarily larger cells. The passage states: 'It is only necessary to call attention to the fact that such collections of cells may form organisms so tiny as to be barely visible to the eye; as, for instance, some of the small flowerless plants or many of the tiny animals living in fresh water or salt water.' The passage also states: 'On the other hand, among animals, the bulk of the elephant and whale, and among plants the big trees of California, stand out as notable examples.' The passage states: 'The large plants and animals are made up of more, not necessarily larger, cells.'
cards.source_quote: It is only necessary to call attention to the fact that such collections of cells may form organisms so tiny as to be barely visible to the. eye; as, for instance, some of the small flowerless plants or many of the tiny animals living in fresh water or salt water.

cards.front: What are some examples of large organisms mentioned in the passage?
cards.back: The big trees of California and the bulk of the elephant and whale are examples of large organisms mentioned in the passage.
cards.source_quote: On the other hand, among animals, the bulk of the elephant and whale, and among plants the big trees of California, stand out as notable examples.

cards.front: What does the passage say about the size of cells in large organisms?
cards.back: The large plants and animals are made up of more, not necessarily larger, cells.
cards.source_quote: The large plants and animals are made up of more, not necessarily larger, cells.

cards.cloze_text: Plant cells and animal cells may live alone, or they may form collections of {{c1::cells}}.
cards.source_quote: Plant cells and animal cells may live alone, or they may form collections of cells.

cards.cloze_text: Some plants are so simple in structure as to be formed of only one kind of {{c1::cells}}.
cards.source_quote: Some plants are so simple in structure as to be formed of only one kind of cells.

cards.cloze_text: Usually living organisms are composed of several groups of different kinds of {{c1::cells}}.
cards.source_quote: Usually living organisms are composed of several groups of different kinds of cells.

cards.cloze_text: Among animals, the bulk of the {{c1::elephant}} and whale, and among plants the big trees of California, stand out as notable examples.

cards.front: What does protoplasm respond to in terms of stimulation?
cards.back: Influences or stimulation from without its own substance, such as light, heat, cold, chemical substances, gravity, and electricity. Both plants and animals are sensitive to touch or stimulation by these factors. Green plants turn toward the source of light; some animals are attracted to light and others repelled by it, like the earthworm. Protoplasm is thus said to be irritable. (Source: What Protoplasm can Do.)
cards.source_quote: What Protoplasm can Do.--It responds to influences or stimulation from without its own substance. Both plants and animals are sensitive to touch or stimulation by light, heat or cold, certain chemical substances, gravity, and electricity. Green plants turn toward the source of light. Some animals are attracted to light and others repelled by it; the earthworm is an example of the latter. _Protoplasm is thus said to be irritable._

cards.front: What is an example of protoplasm being irritable?
cards.back: The earthworm is an example of being repelled by light, demonstrating protoplasm's irritability.

cards.back: Contract and move.
cards.source_quote: Protoplasm has the power to contract and to move. Muscular movement is a familiar instance of this power. Movement may also take place in plants. Some plants fold up their leaves at night; others, like the sensitive plant, fold their leaflets when touched.

cards.front: What is the process by which food materials are absorbed into the cells of the living organism?
cards.back: Protoplasm can form new living matter out of food. To do this, food materials must be absorbed into the cells of the living organism.

cards.front: What chemical elements must enter into the composition of food substances to make protoplasm?
cards.back: The same chemical elements must enter into the composition of the food substances as are found in living matter.
cards.source_quote: it is evident that the same chemical elements must enter into the composition of the food substances as are found in living matter.

cards.front: What do the simplest plants and animals have?
cards.back: This wonderful power as certainly developed as the most complex forms of life.
cards.source_quote: The simplest plants and animals have this wonderful power as certainly developed as the most complex forms of life.

cards.cloze_text: Protoplasm, be it in plant or animal, {{c1::breathes}} and throws off waste materials.
cards.source_quote: _Protoplasm, be it in plant or animal, breathes and throws off waste materials._

cards.cloze_text: When a living thing does work, oxygen unites with food in the body; the food is {{c1::burned}} or oxidized and work is done by means of the energy released from the food.
cards.source_quote: When a living thing does work oxygen unites with food in the body; the food is burned or oxidized and work is done by means of the energy released from the food.

cards.cloze_text: Plants and animals alike pass off the carbon dioxide which results from the {{c1::oxidation}} of food and of parts of their own bodies.
cards.source_quote: Plants and animals alike pass off the carbon dioxide which results from the oxidation of food and of parts of their own bodies.

cards.cloze_text: Animals eliminate wastes containing nitrogen through the {{c1::skin}} and the kidneys.
cards.source_quote: Animals eliminate wastes containing nitrogen through the skin and the kidneys.

cards.front: What is the process by which waste materials are excreted or passed out?
cards.back: Excretion or passing out.
cards.source_quote: The waste materials are excreted or passed out.

cards.front: What is the process that plants and animals perform to form new living things?
cards.back: Reproduction is the final process that plants and animals are called upon to perform. Without the formation of new living things no progress would be possible on the earth. We have found that insects help flowering plants in this process. Let us now see exactly what happens when pollen is placed by the bee on the stigma of another flower of the same kind. To understand this process of reproduction in flowers, we must first study carefully pollen grains from the anther of some growing flower. (Source: The Importance of Reproduction.)
cards.source_quote: Reproduction is the final process that plants and animals are called upon to perform.

cards.front: How do new plants appear?
cards.back: New plants are constantly appearing to take the places of those that die.
cards.source_quote: New plants are constantly appearing to take the places of those that die.

cards.front: What happens to the supply of living things on Earth?
cards.back: The supply of living things upon the earth is not decreasing; reproduction is constantly taking place.
cards.source_quote: The supply of living things upon the earth is not decreasing; reproduction is constantly taking place.

cards.front: What is the role of insects in the process of reproduction for flowering plants?
cards.back: Insects help flowering plants in this process.
cards.source_quote: We have found that insects help flowering plants in this process.

cards.cloze_text: Reproduction is the {{c1::final}} process that plants and animals are called upon to perform.
cards.source_quote: Reproduction is the final process that plants and animals are called upon to perform.

cards.cloze_text: New plants are constantly appearing to take the places of those that die. {{c1::The supply of living things upon the earth is not decreasing; reproduction is constantly taking place.}}
cards.source_quote: The supply of living things upon the earth is not decreasing; reproduction is constantly taking place.

cards.cloze_text: Reproduction is the process that plants and animals are called upon to perform to {{c1::form new living things}}.
cards.source_quote: Without the formation of new living things no progress would be possible on the earth.

cards.cloze_text: To understand this process of reproduction in flowers, we must first study carefully {{c1::pollen grains from the anther}} of some growing flower.
cards.source_quote: To understand this process of reproduction in flowers, we must first study carefully pollen grains from the anther of some growing flower.

cards.front: What are pollen grains of different flowers seen under a microscope?
cards.back: They differ greatly in form and appearance, with some being large, small, rough, smooth, spherical, or angular.
cards.source_quote: Pollen grains of various flowers, when seen under the microscope, differ greatly in form and appearance.

cards.front: What is the structure of pollen grains?
cards.back: They have a thick wall with a thin membrane under it, enclosing a mass of protoplasm.
cards.source_quote: They all agree, however, in having a thick wall, with a thin membrane under it, the whole inclosing a mass of protoplasm.

cards.front: How many cells does a pollen grain contain at an early stage?
cards.back: One cell
cards.source_quote: At an early stage the pollen grain contains but a single cell.

cards.front: What happens to pollen grains after a little time?
cards.back: Two nuclei may be found in the protoplasm, indicating at least two cells.
cards.source_quote: A little later, however, two nuclei may be found in the protoplasm.

cards.cloze_text: Pollen grains of various flowers, when seen under the microscope, {{c1::differ greatly in form and appearance}}.
cards.source_quote: Pollen grains of various flowers, when seen under the microscope, differ greatly in form and appearance.

cards.cloze_text: They all agree, however, in having a thick wall, with a thin membrane under it, the whole {{c1::inclosing a mass of protoplasm}}.
cards.source_quote: They all agree, however, in having a thick wall, with a thin membrane under it, the whole inclosing a mass of protoplasm.

cards.cloze_text: At an early stage the pollen grain contains but a {{c1::single cell}}.
cards.source_quote: At an early stage the pollen grain contains but a single cell.

cards.cloze_text: A little later, however, two {{c1::nuclei}} may be found in the protoplasm.
cards.source_quote: A little later, however, two nuclei may be found in the protoplasm.

cards.front: What is the name of the threadlike mass of protoplasm that grows from a germinated pollen grain?
cards.back: pollen tube
cards.source_quote: The presence of this sugar solution was sufficient to induce growth. When the pollen grain germinates, the nuclei enter the threadlike growth (this growth is called the pollen tube; see Figure).

cards.front: What is the purpose of the sugar solution in the laboratory experiment with pollen grains?
cards.back: To induce growth
cards.source_quote: The presence of this sugar solution was sufficient to induce growth.

cards.front: What is the name of the nuclei that grow into the pollen tube?
cards.back: sperm nuclei
cards.source_quote: One of the nuclei which grows into the pollen tube is known as the sperm nucleus.

cards.cloze_text: Under certain conditions a pollen grain will grow or {{c1::germinate}}.
cards.source_quote: Growth of Pollen Grains.--Under certain conditions a pollen grain will grow or germinate.

cards.cloze_text: The presence of this {{c1::sugar solution}} was sufficient to induce growth.
cards.source_quote: The presence of this sugar solution was sufficient to induce growth.

cards.cloze_text: One of the nuclei which grows into the pollen tube is known as the {{c1::sperm nucleus}}.
cards.source_quote: One of the nuclei which grows into the pollen tube is known as the sperm nucleus.

cards.front: How is the pollen tube formed?
cards.back: From the pollen grain
cards.source_quote: When the pollen grain germinates, the nuclei enter the threadlike growth (this growth is called the pollen tube; see Figure).

cards.front: What is the condition for pollen grain growth in the laboratory experiment?
cards.back: Sprinkling pollen from well-opened flowers of sweet pea or nasturtium on a solution of 15 parts of sugar to 100 of water
cards.source_quote: This growth can be artificially produced in the laboratory by sprinkling pollen from well-opened flowers of sweet pea or nasturtium on a solution of 15 parts of sugar to 100 of water.

cards.front: What is the structure that produces pollen?
cards.back: Anther (a in the illustration)
cards.source_quote: a, anther

cards.front: What is the structure that holds the pollen grain?
cards.back: Pollen grain (pg in the illustration)
cards.source_quote: pg, pollen grain

cards.front: What is the structure that receives the pollen tube?
cards.back: Ovule (o in the illustration)
cards.source_quote: o, ovary

cards.front: What is the structure that contains the egg cell?
cards.back: Ovule (o in the illustration)
cards.source_quote: e, egg cell

cards.front: What is the structure that allows the pollen tube to enter the ovule?
cards.back: Micropyle (m in the illustration)
cards.source_quote: m, micropyle

cards.front: What is the structure that is the opening for the pollen tube to enter the ovule?
cards.back: Micropyle (m in the illustration)
cards.source_quote: m, micropyle

cards.cloze_text: The pollen tube ({{c1::pt}}) enters the ovule through the {{c2::micropyle}} (m) to reach the egg cell (e).
The structure that produces pollen is the {{c1::anther}} (a) and the structure that contains the egg cell is the {{c2::ovule}} (o).

cards.front: What is the primary reason for the existence of a flower?
cards.back: To produce seeds from which future plants will grow
cards.source_quote: _The primary reason for the existence of a flower is that it may produce seeds from which future plants will grow._

cards.front: What happens to the ovule after fertilization?
cards.back: It grows into a seed
cards.source_quote: _After fertilization the ovule grows into a seed._

cards.front: When does the first beginning of growth of the seed take place?
cards.back: At the moment of fertilization
cards.source_quote: _The first beginning of the growth of the seed takes place at the moment of fertilization._

cards.front: What is formed from the growth of the fertilized egg within the ovule?
cards.back: An embryo
cards.source_quote: _From that time on there is a growth of the fertilized egg within the ovule which makes a baby plant called the embryo._

cards.front: What will the embryo give rise to?
cards.back: The adult plant
cards.source_quote: _The embryo will give rise to the adult plant._

cards.front: What is a fruit defined as?
cards.back: a ripened ovary and its contents together with any parts of the flower that may be attached to it
cards.source_quote: a fruit is a ripened ovary and its contents together with any parts of the flower that may be attached to it

cards.front: What is the chief use of the fruit to the flower?
cards.back: to hold and to protect the seeds; it may ultimately distribute them where they can reproduce young plants
cards.source_quote: The chief use of the fruit to the flower is to hold and to protect the seeds; it may ultimately distribute them where they can reproduce young plants.

cards.cloze_text: By definition, {{c1::a fruit is a ripened ovary and its contents together with any parts of the flower that may be attached to it}}
cards.source_quote: By definition, _a fruit is a ripened ovary and its contents together with any parts of the flower that may be attached to it_.

cards.front: What part of the flower becomes the fleshy part of the fruit?
cards.back: the sepals (s) and receptacle
cards.source_quote: Certain outer parts of the flower, the sepals (s) and receptacle, become the fleshy part of the fruit

cards.front: What part of the flower becomes the core of the fruit?
cards.back: the ovary
cards.source_quote: the ovary becomes the core

cards.cloze_text: The pod of a bean, pea, or locust illustrates well the growth from the {{c1::flower}}.
cards.source_quote: The pod of a bean, pea, or locust illustrates well the growth from the flower.

cards.front: What is the pod of a bean, pea, or locust considered to be?
cards.back: a fruit
cards.source_quote: The pod, which is in reality a ripened ovary with other parts of the pistil attached to it, is considered as a fruit.

cards.cloze_text: The pod is in reality a ripened {{c1::ovary}} with other parts of the pistil attached to it.
cards.source_quote: The pod, which is in reality a ripened ovary with other parts of the pistil attached to it, is considered as a fruit.

cards.front: What is the chief reason for flowers from the plant's standpoint?
cards.back: To produce fruits which contain seeds
cards.source_quote: the chief reason for flowers, from the plant's standpoint, is to produce fruits which contain seeds.

cards.front: Why is reproduction and the ultimate scattering of fruits and seeds necessary for plants?
cards.back: To allow colonies of plants to reach new localities
cards.source_quote: Reproduction and the ultimate scattering of fruits and seeds are absolutely necessary in order that colonies of plants may reach new localities.

cards.front: What do plants best fitted to scatter their seeds do?
cards.back: Spread most rapidly
cards.source_quote: It is evident that plants best fitted to scatter their seeds, or place fruits containing the seeds some little distance from the parent plants, are the ones which will spread most rapidly.

cards.front: What must a plant do to advance into new territory?
cards.back: Get its seeds there first
cards.source_quote: A plant, if it is to advance into new territory, must get its seeds there first.

cards.front: Which plants are the most widely distributed on the earth?
cards.back: Plants which are best fitted to scatter their seeds
cards.source_quote: Plants which are best fitted to do this are the most widely distributed on the earth.
